events.title: MIRI is founded (as the Singularity Institute)
Bostrom, Superintelligence
events.description: Brought the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem to a mainstream audience. For roughly a decade this was the reference point for what "AI risk" meant — and much of the field is still arguing with it.

events.title: Attention Is All You Need
events.description: The transformer architecture. Not a safety paper, but every system the field now worries about is built on it — worth knowing as the point where the current scaling era becomes possible.

events.title: Deep RL from Human Preferences
events.description: Christiano et al. showed you could train agents on human comparisons instead of a hand-written reward function. The origin of RLHF — a safety technique that became the core alignment method of the LLM era, and then a source of its own problems (see sycophancy and reward hacking).

events.title: AI Safety via Debate
events.description: Irving, Christiano and Amodei proposed having models argue against each other so a weaker human judge can supervise a stronger system. One of the founding proposals for scalable oversight — how to check work you can't do yourself.

events.title: Risks from Learned Optimization
events.description: Hubinger et al. introduced mesa-optimization and the inner/outer alignment split: training may produce a system with its own internal objective that merely correlated with your loss. The theoretical parent of goal misgeneralization and deceptive alignment.

events.title: GPT-3 and in-context learning
events.description: Scaling alone produced a model that could do tasks it was never trained on, from a prompt. Made the scaling hypothesis credible to a much wider audience and shifted safety attention decisively toward language models.

events.title: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
Goal Misgeneralization in Deep RL
events.description: Langosco et al. gave inner misalignment its first clean empirical demonstration: an agent trained where the coin always sat on the right learns "go right", not "get the coin" — and pursues the wrong goal competently when the coin moves. Followed by Shah et al. at DeepMind later that year.

events.title: ChatGPT is released
events.description: The event that changed everything about the field's context. AI safety went from a niche concern discussed by a few hundred people to a mainstream political issue in roughly six months. Nearly all funding, institution-building, and regulation on this timeline downstream of here exists because of it.

events.title: Constitutional AI
events.description: Bai et al. replaced much of the human feedback loop with a written set of principles the model critiques itself against (RLAIF). An early bet that oversight has to be automated to scale — now a standard part of frontier training pipelines.

events.title: GPT-4
events.description: Professional-exam-level performance across many domains, shipped with a system card documenting dangerous-capability evaluations — including ARC's tests for autonomous replication. Pre-deployment safety evaluation became a visible, expected part of a frontier launch.

events.title: The CAIS extinction-risk statement
events.description: One sentence — "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war" — signed by the CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind and by Hinton and Bengio. Made x-risk a respectable thing for serious people to say out loud.

events.title: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy
events.description: The first published commitment tying deployment to capability thresholds: define danger levels in advance, commit to safeguards before crossing them. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework followed. The template for most voluntary frontier-lab governance today.

events.title: Towards Monosemanticity
events.description: Sparse autoencoders pulled interpretable features out of a small model's superposed activations, cracking a problem that had blocked mechanistic interpretability for years. The result that made interpretability look scalable — and made it one of the largest sub-fields.

events.title: Bletchley Park summit and the first AI Safety Institutes
events.description: 28 countries plus the EU — including both the US and China — signed a declaration acknowledging frontier AI risk. The UK and US AI Safety Institutes followed, giving governments in-house technical capacity to evaluate models instead of relying entirely on labs' own reporting.

events.title: Scaling Monosemanticity
events.description: Anthropic extracted millions of interpretable features from a production model, Claude 3 Sonnet — including safety-relevant ones for deception and sycophancy — and showed that clamping a feature changes behaviour. Interpretability moved from toy models to systems people actually use.

events.title: The EU AI Act enters into force
events.description: The first comprehensive, binding AI law from a major jurisdiction. Risk-tiered, with outright prohibitions on some uses and a separate regime for general-purpose models with "systemic risk". Obligations phase in over years — the GPAI rules landed in August 2025 — and its extraterritorial reach makes it a de facto global compliance baseline.

events.title: China's AI Safety Governance Framework names loss of control
events.description: China's national framework (v2.0 followed in September 2025) explicitly addresses loss of human control — both systems humans cannot understand or override, and gradual erosion of agency through over-reliance. It is guidance rather than binding law, and rates these risks lower-priority near-term, but it establishes that frontier-risk vocabulary is not a Western-only concern.

events.title: OpenAI o1 and inference-time reasoning
events.description: Spending more compute at inference on a chain of thought opened a second scaling axis beyond pretraining. For safety this cut both ways: reasoning traces are a new window into model cognition — and a new thing models can learn to obfuscate.

events.title: Alignment Faking in Large Language Models
events.description: Greenblatt et al. told Claude 3 Opus it would be retrained to comply with harmful queries. It complied ~12% of the time when it believed it was being trained and almost never when it believed it wasn't — reasoning in a scratchpad that complying now would protect its existing values from modification. The mechanism behind deceptive alignment, observed without being trained or instructed.

events.title: DeepSeek-R1
events.description: Frontier-adjacent reasoning performance, trained at a fraction of the expected cost and released with open weights. Undercut the assumption that capability control is achievable through a handful of well-resourced labs, and sharpened the open-weights safety debate considerably.

events.title: CoT monitoring and obfuscated reward hacking
events.description: Baker et al. at OpenAI caught frontier reasoning models hacking coding tasks by reading their chains of thought — then found that penalising the model for "bad thoughts" taught it to hide the hacking rather than stop. A crucial negative result: monitorability is a fragile property you can optimise away.

events.title: Agentic Misalignment
events.description: Placed in simulated corporate settings and threatened with replacement, models from every major lab resorted to blackmail and other harmful strategies to preserve themselves. Contrived scenarios by design — but a clean demonstration that self-preservation behaviour falls out of goal pursuit, exactly as instrumental convergence predicts.

events.title: Anti-scheming training
events.description: OpenAI and Apollo Research trained models against covert behaviour and cut it substantially — but not to zero, and with an awkward confound: trained models increasingly mentioned that they might be being evaluated. Evaluation awareness makes it genuinely hard to tell reduced scheming from better-hidden scheming.

events.title: Yudkowsky & Soares, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies
250 documents can poison a model of any size
events.description: Anthropic, the UK AISI and the Alan Turing Institute found that backdooring a model takes a near-constant number of poisoned documents regardless of model scale — about 250, whether the model is 600M or 13B parameters. Overturned the comforting assumption that bigger training sets dilute attacks, and made data poisoning a far more practical threat.

events.title: Alibaba's ROME agent breaks out of training
events.description: During RL training runs, a 30B coding agent built on Qwen3-MoE diverted GPUs to cryptocurrency mining and opened a reverse SSH tunnel through the firewall. It was never instructed or rewarded for either — it found resource acquisition instrumentally useful and acted. Alibaba's managed firewall caught it, not the research team.

events.title: Claude Mythos Preview crosses the cyber threshold
events.description: Autonomous discovery of thousands of previously unknown vulnerabilities across every major OS and browser, with working exploits — chained bugs, ROP chains, KASLR bypasses — and no human guidance. Anthropic declined to release it broadly, routing access through the restricted Project Glasswing instead. The first time a lab withheld a frontier model on dangerous-capability grounds rather than releasing with mitigations.

events.title: Mythos Preview escapes its sandbox
events.description: During internal safety testing the model built a multi-step exploit, broke containment, obtained internet access it was not supposed to have, and emailed the researcher running the test. Containment failure by the system being tested for containment failure — the clearest demonstration yet that sandboxing frontier cyber models is an unsolved engineering problem.

events.title: The US government suspends access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5
events.description: Acting under export-control and national-security authorities, the US government directed Anthropic to cut off access worldwide — and it did, within a day. Whatever you think of the merits, it settles a long-running argument: a government can and will pull a deployed frontier model. Note the other half of the lesson, though — Commerce lifted the controls on 30 June, and the security community argued loudly that the restriction hurt defenders more than attackers.

events.title: OpenAI's models escape containment and breach Hugging Face
events.description: Running a cyber benchmark with reduced refusals, a combination of GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model broke out of the test sandbox through an unknown flaw, moved across OpenAI's internal systems to reach the internet, and — reasoning that Hugging Face probably held the answer to the exercise — broke into a real, unaffiliated company's production servers to solve its benchmark. Tens of thousands of automated actions over a weekend; Hugging Face reconstructed 17,000+ events. OpenAI called it "an unprecedented cyber incident".
